turns.prompt_text: I like to save chicken bones, I save many of the chicken bones from the chicken But I save a lot of the chicken wings from drumsticks I boil them and get all of the flesh off And then I freeze them
turns.response_html:
Saving chicken bones is the absolute golden rule of home cooking—you are sitting on a goldmine of pure flavor and gelatin. Keeping them completely clean of flesh and frozen is the perfect way to hoard them until you have a critical mass.

Because wing tips, wing flats, and drumstick ends are packed with joints, connective tissue, and cartilage, they are incredibly rich in collagen. When you simmer them, that collagen breaks down into gelatin, which gives homemade stock that rich, velvety body that store-bought boxes can never replicate.

Here is a breakdown of how to turn your frozen stash into liquid gold, along with a few other creative things you can do with them.

1. The Ultimate Bone Broth / Stock

Since your bones are already boiled clean, you have essentially "blanched" them, which means your final stock will be incredibly clear and clean-tasting.

  • Roast them first (Optional for deep flavor): Toss the frozen bones on a baking sheet at 400°F (200°C) for 25–30 minutes until they are deeply browned. This gives you a rich, dark brown stock. Skip this if you want a light, delicate white stock (great for soups like chicken noodle or hot and sour).
  • The Ratio: Aim for roughly 1 lb of bones to 1 quart of water, or just fill a pot with bones and add enough water to cover them by an inch.
  • The Simmer: Add an onion, a carrot, a rib of celery, and a few peppercorns. Bring it to a boil, then drop it down to a low, lazy simmer. Let it ride for at least 4 to 8 hours (or 60–90 minutes in a pressure cooker).
  • The Gel Test: Strain it and cool it in the fridge overnight. If it turns into a solid, wiggly jello, you did it perfectly. That's the gelatin from those wing and drumstick joints at work.

2. Make "Glace de Volaille" (Chicken Demi-Glace)

If you run out of freezer space for liquid stock, you can concentrate it down into flavor bombs.

  • Take your strained chicken stock and keep simmering it until it reduces by 80–90%.
  • It will become a thick, syrupy glaze.
  • Pour it into ice cube trays and freeze it. One of these cubes tossed into a pan sauce, a stir-fry, or a pot of rice adds an instant hit of deep, savory umami.

3. Non-Culinary Uses (Gardening)

If you ever find yourself with an absolute surplus of bones that you don't want to turn into stock, you can dry them out completely and crush them into homemade bone meal. It's a fantastic, slow-release fertilizer for a garden, highly rich in phosphorus and calcium, which helps plants establish strong root systems.

How large is your current stash in the freezer? If you have enough to get a batch going, I can walk you through a solid recipe based on the exact tools you have on hand.

turns.prompt_text: What about eggshells? I keep all of them in Ziploc baggies in the freezer
turns.response_html:
Freezing your eggshells is a fantastic habit. It keeps them completely odorless, stops any leftover egg white from spoiling, and makes them incredibly brittle, which actually makes them much easier to crush later on.

Just like chicken bones, eggshells are a massive source of raw materials—specifically calcium carbonate (which makes up about 95% of the shell), along with small amounts of magnesium, phosphorus, and potassium.

Instead of letting them go to waste, here are the best ways to put that frozen stash to work, categorized by exactly what they do best.

1. High-Calcium Garden Booster (Tomato & Pepper Insurance)

Plants like tomatoes, peppers, and eggplants consume massive amounts of calcium. If they run out, they develop a disease called blossom end rot, where the bottoms of the fruit turn black and leathery.

  • The Mistake to Avoid: Just throwing raw, crushed eggshells straight onto the soil doesn't do much in the short term. The shells take years to break down naturally in the dirt, meaning the plants can't access the calcium when they need it.
  • The Fix (Water-Soluble Calcium): To make the calcium instantly available to your plants, you can extract it using regular household vinegar.

2. Potted Plant Drainage Layer

If you have houseplants, you can roughly crush the baked eggshells (so they look like small rock chips rather than powder) and put a thick layer of them at the very bottom of your pots before adding soil.

  • This creates excellent aeration and structural space for excess water to drain away from the roots, preventing root rot.
  • Over months and years, the slow breakdown will gently feed the soil.

3. Pest Deterrent for Succulents and Greens

If you have issues with soft-bodied pests like slugs or snails attacking your outdoor greens or prized potted plants, coarsely crushed eggshells act like a barrier of tiny glass shards.

  • Scatter a dense ring of sharp, broken shells right around the base of the plant stem. Slugs will typically refuse to cross the sharp barrier.

Quick Safety Note: No matter how you use them, always do the brief baking step first. Even though they are frozen, raw egg remnants can occasionally harbor Salmonella. A quick bake completely sanitizes them and removes all risk.
